_about: Research content for /football/research (M2 §33). Rendered by scripts/build_research.py. Prose comes from the Final Summary (docs/Football Research Series — Final Summary.pdf); chart values are read from football/data/research.json at build time. Inline markup: {glossary-key|label} = glossary term, **bold**, *italic*. Charts: a string is a builder id computed from research.json; an object is an inline chart for results with no data export (Study 1), always with a source.
sources: Understat · football-data.co.uk · Open-Meteo ERA5 · Wikipedia/Wikidata · OpenStreetMap

index.title: What actually belongs to the player?
index.lede: Five studies investigating how much football performance belongs to the player — and how much belongs to the context.
index.spine_lede: Each study builds on the one before. The first three remove context from the numbers; the last two use the cleaned numbers to compare players and follow them across leagues.
fit: Study 1 asked whether the environment moves performance — weather barely, crowds much more (home advantage roughly halved without fans). Study 2 took the crowd effect to the individual: home advantage is real, large and shared by everyone. Study 3 did the same for opposition: large, shared, with no individual “big-game” trait.

Together they gave clean, context-adjusted player numbers. Study 4 used those numbers to find similar players across leagues, and found the limit: similarity describes, it does not forecast. Study 5 tested forecasting directly on real transfers and built a validated, leakage-free model of how much output survives a move — in which similarity had to earn its place and did not.
index.lessons_title: Five lessons that run through everything
lessons: Context moves the numbers, and it moves everyone the same.

Home, crowd and opposition effects are large, but they belong to the match and the league, not to individual players or clubs. Every “special” player we looked for — home specialists, big-game players, crowd-sensitive players — disappeared once noise was separated from signal.
Most apparent individual differences are small samples.

A player's home/away split is only 5–8% signal, and his strong/weak-opponent split is mostly noise; raw rankings of these traits are {regression-to-the-mean|regression to the mean} in action (Study 2: the correlation between players' 2015–19 and 2022–25 home edges is 0.018).
A player's overall level is the best predictor of almost everything.

His overall opponent-adjusted output predicts his output against elite teams better than his record against elite teams (Study 3); his own pre-move history predicts his post-move output better than similar players do (Studies 4 and 5).
Similarity is a discovery tool, not a forecasting tool.
Comparable players help find candidates; they add nothing to a forecast once the player's own history is known (Study 5, critical experiment).

Understat's match “forecast” turned out to be post-match; it was never used. Opponent strength is built only from pre-match odds; every Study 5 prediction uses only information available at the decision date, and the final model was scored once on {locked-test|locked seasons}.
index.corrections_lede: The interesting result isn't always the first one. These are the readings we changed along the way.
corrections: Understat's win/draw/loss “forecast” was at first described as pre-match; it is post-match (r = 0.96 with the match's xG difference). It was never used in any model.
Study 2's “stable part” magnitudes are upper bounds: the cross-season covariance estimator is biased upward even with no true persistence (found in Study 3). Conclusions unchanged.
Study 5: a promoted-club term was first read as an imputation artefact; it is a real effect (players joining promoted clubs produce more than the club's rating predicts).
Study 5: the early “centre-forwards drop most” reading was mostly regression to the mean (96% vs stayers, no clear role effect).
open: Study 1's hand-written weather conclusion and freeze.
Study 5's percentage-based league effect, to be validated on moves after 2025/26.

meta.title: Research · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Five studies on 525,328 player-matches from Europe's top five leagues: environment, home advantage, opposition, similarity and transferability — one investigation into what belongs to the player.

studies.title: Weather, crowds and player performance
studies.question: Does the environment change the player?
studies.subquestion: Do weather and crowds change how much a player produces?
status_parts: Survives the placebo check · conclusion pending
studies.status_note: The five-league weather models and the final 1,000-permutation temperature placebo check finished on 6 October 2026. The hand-written weather conclusion and the freeze are still to come, so the weather answer on this page is provisional. The crowd results are final.
studies.summary: Weather barely changes how much players produce: with all five leagues, rain and humidity effects sit within about ±2%, and wind is small (about −1% per +10 km/h). Crowds appear to: empty stadiums roughly halved home advantage, and it came back with the fans.

body: If rain, wind or heat changed what players produce, every raw stat line would carry the weather with it, and a player's numbers would partly depend on the climate he plays in.
Crowds are the same question with people instead of weather: does a full stadium change what happens on the pitch?
why.question: Does the environment a match is played in move player numbers?

method.plain: Each player is compared with himself — wet days against dry, full stadiums against empty — so differences in ability and team quality never enter the comparison.
technical: Weather: {ppml|PPML} on per-minute output with player × season, opponent × season, league × kickoff-hour and league × season × month {fixed-effects|fixed effects}; ERA5 weather at the stadium and kickoff hour. A player × team × season version moves no estimate by more than 0.6 percentage points.

Crowds: team-level PPML with team × season and opponent × season fixed effects; 13,888 matches with fans and 1,893 behind closed doors, partial crowds excluded. Crowd status from a dated, sourced calendar per league.

Six hypotheses fixed before looking (rain and long shots, wind and headers/crosses, heat and late-game output). {multiple-testing|Benjamini–Hochberg corrections} on cluster and {permutation-test|permutation} p-values; {placebo|placebo tests} with the closed-doors dates shifted 2–4 years.

findings.title: Crowds
Without fans, home advantage shrank — and came back with them.
findings.lead: The pooled xG home edge went from **+30%** with fans before 2020 to **+13%** behind closed doors, then back to **+26%** when crowds returned.

chart.title: Pooled team xG home edge, by period
chart.sub: Home ÷ away, team level, all five leagues.
chart.words: The xG home edge fell from +30% (with fans, before 2020) to +13% without crowds and recovered to +26% when they returned.

findings.explain: Every league lost xG home advantage without fans; Ligue 1 lost its whole goals edge.

findings.title: Without fans, the home edge shrank on every measure.
findings.lead: Home ÷ away at team level: goals **1.27 → 1.11**, {xg|xG} **1.29 → 1.13**, shots **1.23 → 1.13**. Yellow cards went from **0.89** (home side booked less) to **1.02** — the advantage gone.

chart.title: Home ÷ away, with fans vs behind closed doors
chart.words: Every attacking ratio moved toward 1.00 without fans, and the home side's lighter treatment in yellow cards disappeared.

findings.title: Weather
findings.status_label: Models and placebo check done · conclusion and freeze pending

findings.title: Weather barely changes how much players produce.
findings.lead: With all five leagues, rain and humidity effects on shots, xG, xA, goals and key passes sit within about **±2%**. Wind is small but now detectable: about **−1%** shots, key passes and xA per +10 km/h. Over ten Premier League seasons alone, **0 of 20** weather × metric effects survived correction.

chart.title: Weather, next to the crowd
chart.sub: Change in output. The shaded band is the range the five-league rain and humidity estimates sit in.
chart.words: Rain and humidity move output by about 2% at most and wind by about 1% — a small fraction of what a crowd does to home advantage.
chart.source: Study 01 · five-league weather run (6 Oct 2026); crowd rows team level

findings.title: Six predictions, written down before looking.
findings.label: pre-registered weather hypotheses survive
findings.lead: Rain and long shots, wind and headers or crosses, heat and late-game output: on five leagues and 445,377 non-penalty shots, none of them held up.

findings.title: Temperature: survives the placebo check
findings.lead: With all five leagues, warmer kickoffs go with slightly more chance creation: per +10 °C, key passes **+3.2%**, xA **+3.2%** and goals **+4.2%** (xG +1.2%, not significant). It survives a 1,000-permutation placebo check and team and stadium controls (a stadium control trims it slightly). It is strongest in Serie A (xA +10.7%, goals +9.3%), present in Ligue 1 and La Liga, and absent in the Premier League and Bundesliga. **A small, league-specific association — the final conclusion is pending review.**

surprise.suggested: Forwards' xA rose 29% in the rain in the 2024/25 Premier League — a promising lead.
surprise.after: On three other leagues the same effect was −1.4%; on all five, −1.2% (p = 0.43). Not replicated.
surprise.lesson: A striking result from one league and one season is a hypothesis, not a finding. It has to replicate.

meaning: For rain, wind and humidity, the weather is not something a player's numbers need correcting for. Temperature is the exception: a small association that survives the placebo check, mostly in Serie A — its final conclusion is pending review.
Crowds are different — and a crowd effect is a home effect. That is where Study 2 picks up.
limitations: The hand-written weather conclusion and the freeze are still pending; the temperature result is provisional until then.
The closed-doors period is mostly one season, so per-player crowd estimates are noisy; there are no attendance figures — only fans or no fans.
Cup matches and fixture congestion are not in the data.
Observational data: effects are associations within carefully matched comparisons.

next.question: If crowds move home advantage, does it belong to individual players?

meta.title: Study 01 · Weather, crowds and player performance · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Study 1: rain and humidity barely change player output (within about ±2% on five leagues); empty stadiums roughly halved home advantage. Final weather conclusion and freeze pending.
meta.og_title: Does the environment change the player?

studies.title: Individual home advantage
studies.question: Does home advantage belong to the player?
studies.subquestion: Which players benefit most from playing at home?
studies.spine_question: How much does playing at home matter?
studies.spine_answer: A lot — and the same for everyone.
studies.summary: Everyone does better at home by about the same amount: +27% xG per minute for the same player, in the same team and season. Not one of 4,665 players has a reliable personal home edge.

body: Home and away splits are one of the first things people reach for: this striker is a home player, that winger travels badly.
If those splits were real, part of a player's value would depend on where he plays — and a transfer would change it.
why.question: Is home advantage a property of the player, or of the match?

method.plain: Comparing a player only with himself removes ability, team quality and season form. What's left is the effect of playing at home.
technical: Within-player {ppml|PPML} on per-minute output with {fixed-effects|player × team × season fixed effects}; errors clustered by match.

Individual effects get calibrated standard errors from pseudo-splits and shuffles within each player's own matches, a DerSimonian–Laird estimate of the real between-player spread, and {shrinkage|empirical-Bayes shrinkage}.
Persistence is measured against shuffled data. {multiple-testing|Benjamini–Hochberg corrections}, {permutation-test|permutation tests} and {placebo|placebo tests} for every headline effect.

findings.title: Everyone gets better at home.
findings.lead: Per minute, for the same player: {xg|xG} **+27%**, {xa|xA} **+25%**, shots **+22%**, {key-passes|key passes} **+21%**, goals **+24%**.
findings.explain: Every attacking number moves together, by roughly a quarter.

findings.title: How big is that? About half of it disappeared without crowds.
findings.lead: Behind closed doors the xG edge fell from **+28%** to **+12%**, and came back to **+25%** with fans. The betting market priced the same loss: the home/away win-probability ratio for evenly matched teams fell from **1.58** to **1.31**.

findings.title: Leagues differ.
findings.lead: La Liga has the largest home edge (xG **+35%**), Serie A the smallest (**+23%**).

findings.title: But do some players have more of it?
findings.intro: Maybe the average is shared, but a few players are genuine home specialists.
findings.label: players with a reliable personal home edge
findings.lead: Each player's estimate is only 5–8% {signal-noise|signal}. Within a team-season, individual differences vanish for xG, shots, key passes and goals.

findings.title: Clubs don't own it either.
findings.lead: Against their own league's average, clubs differ by about **±1%**: **0 of 121** clubs are reliably different, and a club's past home edge does not predict its future one.

surprise.suggested: The 2015–19 “top 10 home players” looked like genuine home specialists.
surprise.after: In 2022–25 they were back near the all-player average: +43%, against +33% for everyone. The correlation between the two periods was 0.018.
surprise.lesson: A home/away split is mostly noise. Ranking players by it is {regression-to-the-mean|regression to the mean} in action.

meaning: Treat home advantage as part of the match, not the player: give every player the same home lift, and don't credit or blame anyone for a home/away split.
On new seasons, the league average is a better forecast of a player's home edge than his own past record (2025/26: r = 0.011).
limitations: The closed-doors period is mostly one season, so per-player crowd effects are noisy; there are no attendance figures.
Study 2's “stable part” magnitudes are upper bounds: the cross-season estimator is biased upward even with no true persistence (found later, in Study 3). Conclusions are unchanged.
Output only — no defending, pace or possession; goalkeepers are excluded.
Observational data: effects are associations within carefully matched comparisons.

next.question: Home is one context. What happens when the opponent gets stronger?

meta.title: Study 02 · Individual home advantage · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Study 2: every player produces about 27% more xG per minute at home, by about the same amount. 0 of 4,665 players have a reliable personal home edge.
meta.og_title: Does home advantage belong to the player?

studies.title: The opposition effect
studies.question: Do some players actually thrive against better teams?
studies.subquestion: How much of a player's output survives when the opponent gets stronger?
studies.spine_question: What happens when the opponent gets stronger?
studies.spine_answer: Everyone drops — by about the same amount.
studies.summary: Player attacking output falls substantially as opponent strength increases — but we found no reliable evidence that some individuals consistently resist that effect.

body: Raw statistics make player comparison deceptively simple. A player who piles up numbers against weak sides isn't necessarily better than one who produces a little less against strong ones.
And if some players really rise to big occasions, that would be worth knowing before a cup final — or a transfer.
why.question: Can we separate player level from opponent difficulty?

method.plain: We're comparing a player's output against different opponents rather than simply comparing raw totals.
technical: {opponent-strength|Opponent strength} is a sequential market rating from pre-match odds: each match uses only earlier matches. Checked against an xG rating, Elo, opening odds and points per game; 0 changed ratings in 155,282 {leakage|leakage} checks.
Within-player {ppml|PPML} with {fixed-effects|player × team × season fixed effects}, plus venue, month and kickoff hour; errors clustered by match.
Individual resistance: calibrated standard errors, between-player spread and {shrinkage|empirical-Bayes shrinkage}; {multiple-testing|Benjamini–Hochberg corrections}.

findings.title: A stronger opponent hurts everyone.
findings.lead: {xg|xG} falls **13.8%** for every +1 {sd|SD} increase in {opponent-strength|opponent strength}.
findings.explain: Same player, team and season, after accounting for venue: {xa|xA} −15.1%, shots −10.5%, key passes −11.4%, goals −15.8%.

findings.title: How big is that?
findings.lead: Against the strongest fifth of opponents, xG is **33% lower** than against the weakest fifth (xA −35%).

findings.title: The same in every position.
findings.lead: The effect is the same across positions and home/away, and unchanged behind closed doors — unlike home advantage.

findings.title: Leagues differ a little.
findings.lead: Steepest in Serie A (xG **−16%**, xA **−18%** per SD). In La Liga and Ligue 1, shot and key-pass volume barely drops against strong sides (about −7% to −8%).

findings.title: But are some players different?
findings.intro: Maybe the average effect is strong, but certain players are unusually resistant to elite opposition.
findings.label: player × metric estimates show reliable resistance
findings.lead: We found no reliable individual player × metric estimates showing consistent resistance to stronger opposition. Season-to-season correlation of a player's “resistance”: **0.012**.

findings.title: The practical rule.
findings.lead: To predict a player's output against elite opponents, use his overall opponent-adjusted level, not his record against elite teams: xG **r 0.84 vs 0.75**.

findings.title: Adjusting a season changes little — except where it matters.
findings.lead: Season adjustments are typically **±2%** because everyone plays everyone twice; up to ±10% for players used unevenly, e.g. Callum Wilson 2023/24 (**−9.9%**). Bruno Fernandes's elite chance creation survives: **0.467 → 0.460** xA per 90 in 2022/23, 99.6th percentile.
findings.explain: Adjustment matters most for partial seasons, single matches and cross-league comparisons.

surprise.suggested: In the raw data, about 29% of players look like “flat-track bullies” and about 26% like “big-game players”.
surprise.after: That is exactly what noise produces. With proper intervals, one player in about 4,800 shows a reliable pattern (for shots) — what chance alone would produce — and after correcting for multiple tests, none of the 23,022 estimates survives.
surprise.lesson: Raw “big-game” records look like context and noise: the research found no evidence of a stable player trait.

meaning: Opposition is one of the biggest contexts in the numbers. Adjust for it — especially for partial seasons, single matches and cross-league comparisons.
To judge how a player will do against elite teams, look at his overall adjusted level.
limitations: Opponent strength is the betting market's pre-match view of a team; it is validated against four alternatives, but it is still a rating, not a fact.
Output only — the data cannot see defending, pressing or possession.
Cup matches and fixture congestion are not in the data.
Observational data: effects are associations within carefully matched comparisons.

next.question: With context removed, can we finally compare players — across leagues?

meta.title: Study 03 · The opposition effect · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Study 3: −13.8% xG per +1 SD of opponent strength, the same for everyone. 0 of 23,022 player × metric estimates show reliable resistance.
meta.og_title: Do some players actually thrive against better teams?

studies.title: Cross-league player similarity

turn.before: Studies 1–3 asked: can we remove context?
turn.after: Study 4 asks: now that we've adjusted for context, can we compare players?

studies.question: Who actually plays like whom?
studies.subquestion: Can we find functionally similar players across leagues?
studies.spine_question: Can we find players who actually play alike?
studies.summary: Context-adjusted profiles find sensible matches across leagues — Bruno → Serie A: Samardžić, Dybala, Chukwueze — but nobody matches his chance creation. Similarity describes a player; it is not a forecast.

body: Recruitment often starts with “who plays like him, in a league we can afford?”. Raw numbers can't answer it across leagues: the league, the opponents and the venue all leave fingerprints on a stat line.
Studies 1–3 measured those fingerprints. Now they can be removed.
why.question: Once context is removed, can we find a player's functional twin in another league?

flow: Adjusted for opponent, venue and league
method.plain: Each profile is adjusted for opponent, venue and league, normalized within {role|role}, then compared using {cosine-similarity|cosine similarity}.
technical: Roles come from the data: clustering Understat's granular positions on per-90 output gives seven roles. A central attacking midfielder produces like a wide forward, not like other central midfielders.
Metrics are {z-score|z-scored} within role and compared by cosine similarity; three-season {profile-window|profile windows} are the steadiest.
Validated without opinions by {self-retrieval|self-retrieval}: after a league move, does a player's new profile find his old one?

findings.title: The profile finds the same player again — even after a move.
findings.lead: Three-season profiles find the same player in the **top 9%** of a destination league's role pool after a league move. Adjusted inputs beat raw ones for players who changed league.
findings.explain: Single seasons are noisy profiles; longer windows are steadier.

findings.title: We looked for Bruno's closest statistical profile in Serie A.
findings.lead: Bruno Fernandes's chance creation is **3.6 SD** above his role average. Serie A's best comparable is **1.9 SD**.
findings.callout: None was a true like-for-like Bruno equivalent.
findings.explain: Samardžić, Dybala and Chukwueze are robust matches on the rest of the profile — but every one of them creates less. A high score means two profiles look alike, not that one player is the other.

findings.title: About half of what makes a player distinctive survives a move.
findings.lead: After a real move, the player's own pre-move profile forecasts his new-league output **as well as** his comparables do.

surprise.suggested: A central attacking midfielder sounds like a kind of central midfielder.
surprise.after: On the numbers he produces like a wide forward — so roles were rebuilt from what players produce, not where the team sheet puts them.
surprise.lesson: A position label describes where a player stands. Output describes what he does.

meaning: Similarity is a discovery tool: it finds candidates worth watching in leagues you don't follow.
It is not a forecasting tool. A high score says two profiles look alike — not that one player will produce like the other after a move.
limitations: Output only: the profile cannot see defending, pressing, pace or physical data.
Single seasons are noisy profiles; longer windows are steadier.
Study 4's user-curated “known similar pairs” check is still open.
Similarity scores rank players within a role pool; they are not probabilities.

next.kicker: We had found players who looked similar.
next.question: But does similarity actually tell us what happens next?

meta.title: Study 04 · Cross-league player similarity · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Study 4: context-adjusted, role-normalised profiles find similar players across leagues. Bruno → Serie A: Samardžić, Dybala, Chukwueze — but nobody matches his 3.6 SD chance creation.

studies.title: Transferability
studies.question: Will his game travel?
studies.subquestion: What happens to attacking output when a player changes leagues?
clarify: Transferability asks whether his output survives the move.
studies.spine_question: Can we predict what happens when the player moves?
studies.spine_answer: Partly — from his own history, not from who he resembles.
studies.summary: Most output survives a move on average (97% vs comparable stayers), but one league-difficulty ladder accounts for the direction. A model of the player's own history, age and clubs beats “he'll do what he did” on unseen seasons; similarity adds nothing to it.

body: Every summer, clubs pay for output produced somewhere else. Whether that output travels is the question behind every cross-league signing.
Study 4 can say who a player resembles. It can't say what happens after he moves.
why.question: How much of a player's output survives a league move — and can we predict it?

method.benchmark: We compare movers against {stayers|comparable players who stayed} — same club, role, output and age — so that ordinary {regression-to-the-mean|regression to the mean} isn't mistaken for a transfer effect.
method.plain: Output drops after any strong season, move or no move. Comparing movers with similar players who stayed separates the move from that ordinary drop.
technical: Understat has no transfer records, so moves were inferred from club changes (including deadline-day moves after early matches). Of 2,917 cross-league moves, the primary population is 428 summer moves (2016/17–2025/26) by forwards and midfielders with ≥900 minutes before and after; every exclusion is listed with its reason.
{retention|Retention} = output after ÷ output before (xG + xA per 90). Dates of birth were linked from the CC0 Transfermarkt-derived dataset (100% of the 428 moves).
Every prediction uses only information available at the decision date; the final model was scored once on {locked-test|locked seasons}.

findings.title: On average, most of it survives.
findings.lead: Movers keep **97%** of their output compared with comparable stayers (95% {interval|confidence interval} **93–101%**): an average move costs about 3%.

findings.title: But direction matters most.
findings.lead: One {league-ladder|ladder of league difficulty} fits all 20 directions: moving **into** the Premier League keeps **82%**; moving **out** of it, **117%**.
findings.explain: Premier League hardest, Serie A and La Liga in the middle, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 easiest. Pair-specific effects add nothing (p = 0.91): Serie A → Premier League keeps ~80%, Premier League → Serie A ~114%.

findings.title: Age and the destination club matter too.
findings.lead: Younger players keep more — about **−2% per year** of age (U21 **109%**, 30+ **93%**). The destination club matters as much as the league: weakest third of destination clubs **79%**, strongest third **106%**.
findings.explain: Players coming off a jump in output drop more (−9% per SD of last-season change). No effect: role (once regression to the mean is removed), consistency over three seasons, profile distinctiveness, penalty duties, loans.

findings.title: Can we predict the move?
findings.lead: Each step adds information the naive guess ignores. The final model cuts the error from **0.129** to **0.096** and lifts {r-squared|R²} from **0.58** to **0.76**.

findings.title: The model was frozen before the test.
findings.lead: The final model was fixed before the test seasons and evaluated once on 142 unseen moves. It beat the naive baseline by **0.033** xG + xA per 90 (CI 0.018–0.049) and did slightly better on the unseen seasons than on earlier ones — no sign of overfitting.

findings.title: Similarity had to earn its place. It didn't.
findings.lead: Adding Study 4's similarity — what the most similar destination-league players produce, match quality, distinctiveness, how similar movers fared — changed the error by nothing detectable — at most **0.002** either way (all similarity features together: +0.001, 95% CI −0.002 to +0.005). Comparables alone were worse than the player's own history.

findings.title: A prediction is a range, not a number.
findings.lead: The chance of keeping ≥75% ranks players well ({auc|AUC} **0.80**) and beats a same-for-everyone base rate ({brier|Brier} **0.179 vs 0.224**), and is {calibration|calibrated} at the top. But individual forecasts are uncertain: a typical {range-80|80% range} is **±0.2** xG + xA per 90.
findings.explain: Lower thresholds (50%, 60%) were not well calibrated and are not used.

findings.title: Where the model breaks.
findings.lead: The league effect is a fixed amount, not a percentage, so low-output central midfielders moving into the Premier League are under-predicted by about **0.06** xG + xA per 90.

example.name: Manuel Ugarte
example.context: Manchester United case study, summer 2024 — standing at 1 June 2024 with only what was known then.

findings.explain: Ugarte was bought for defensive work this data cannot see. The model primarily sees attacking output. A percentage-based league effect is the next version.

surprise.suggested: Early on, centre-forwards seemed to drop the most after a move, and a promoted-club effect looked like a data artefact.
surprise.after: Against comparable stayers, centre-forwards keep 96% — mostly regression to the mean, no clear role effect. And the promoted-club effect holds up: players joining promoted clubs produced more than the club's rating predicted.
surprise.lesson: Every raw transfer pattern needs a control group — and a second look.

meaning: To forecast a move, start from the player's own history, age and both clubs, and place both leagues on the difficulty ladder.
Use similarity to find candidates and the transfer model to size the risk — never one as the other.
Read every forecast as a range. The model estimates its own uncertainty; a single number hides that.
limitations: Output only: defending, pace, possession, injuries, fees and contracts are not in the data; defenders and goalkeepers are excluded.
The league effect is fixed rather than proportional — the Ugarte weakness. A percentage-based version is to be validated on moves after 2025/26.
Individual forecasts are uncertain: a typical 80% range is ±0.2 xG + xA per 90.
Observational data: effects are associations within carefully matched comparisons.

next.kicker: Five studies, one answer: context belongs to the match; level belongs to the player.
next.question: Does it still hold on seasons the studies never saw?

meta.title: Study 05 · Transferability · Home Turf & Hard Opponents
meta.description: Study 5: movers keep 97% of their output vs comparable stayers, but the league ladder decides the direction. A history-based model beats the naive guess on 142 locked moves; similarity adds 0.000.
